title: Use verbal communication in extension and development

lessons.title: The communication process and its barriers
lessons.html:
Talking is the core of extension

Most extension takes place through speech: a conversation at the kraal, a talk at a farmers' day, a phone call about a sick cow, a radio slot on a community station. Verbal communication is fast and personal, but it is also easy to misunderstand.

The communication process

  1. Sender - the practitioner or farmer with a message.
  2. Message - the idea, such as when to plant after the first good rains.
  3. Encoding - putting the idea into words, examples and gestures.
  4. Channel - face to face, phone, radio, meeting.
  5. Receiver - the person who decodes the message.
  6. Feedback - the response that shows whether the message was understood.

Communication is a two-way process. Without feedback you do not know if the farmer understood or agreed.

Barriers to verbal communication

  • Language - speaking English to farmers who prefer isiXhosa or Setswana; using technical jargon.
  • Physical - wind, noise from a tractor, a large meeting without a loudhailer.
  • Cultural - customs about who speaks first, respect for elders, eye contact and how men and women address each other.
  • Psychological - distrust of government, fear of looking foolish, fatigue after a long working day.
  • Status - farmers may agree politely with an official without intending to act.

Reducing barriers

Use the listener's language or a reliable interpreter. Choose quiet venues and suitable times. Learn local customs, for example greeting elders first. Check understanding by asking the farmer to explain the advice in their own words rather than asking 'Do you understand?'

lessons.title: Listening, questioning and one-to-one conversations
lessons.html:
Listening is half of communication

Good extension practitioners listen more than they speak. Farmers know their land, animals and constraints; listening reveals the real problem and builds trust.

Active listening skills

  • Give full attention; put the phone away.
  • Show interest with nods and short responses.
  • Paraphrase: 'So you are saying the calves are weak in the first week?'
  • Reflect feelings: 'It sounds as if the losses have been very worrying.'
  • Summarise the main points at the end.
  • Do not interrupt or jump to solutions too quickly.

Questioning techniques

TypeExampleUse
OpenHow do you feed the pigs in winter?Explore and gather information
ClosedDid you dose the sheep this month?Confirm specific facts
ProbingWhat happened after that?Get more detail
LeadingYou do clean the water troughs, don't you?Avoid; it pushes the answer

Farm visits and advisory conversations

  1. Greet properly and build rapport before business.
  2. Clarify the purpose of the visit.
  3. Ask open questions and walk the farm with the farmer.
  4. Discuss options together and agree on actions.
  5. Summarise what was agreed and when you will follow up.

Telephone advice is common. Speak slowly, confirm the farmer's name and location, repeat key instructions and, for animal health or chemical issues, refer to the vet or the product label instead of guessing.

Non-verbal communication

Tone of voice, posture and gestures carry meaning. Standing with arms folded or checking your watch suggests impatience. Dressing practically for the farm shows respect for the setting.

lessons.title: Presentations, meetings and radio
lessons.html:
Speaking to groups

Practitioners often speak at farmers' days, study group meetings and community gatherings, and sometimes on community radio.

Preparing a talk

  1. Know the audience: farming type, language and level of experience.
  2. Set one clear objective, such as farmers being able to identify signs of heartwater.
  3. Limit the talk to three or four key messages.
  4. Use local examples, stories and real objects such as a soil sample or a dosing gun.
  5. Plan time for questions and discussion.

Delivering a talk

  • Stand where everyone can see and hear you; outdoors, keep the sun and wind behind the audience.
  • Speak clearly, vary your tone and make eye contact where culturally appropriate.
  • Use pauses and repeat key messages.
  • Invite farmers to share their own experience.
  • End with a summary and what to do next.

Facilitating meetings

Agree the agenda, keep to time, give everyone a chance to speak, manage dominant speakers politely and summarise decisions. Use an interpreter for mixed-language groups and allow time for translation.

Radio and voice messages

Community radio reaches many rural listeners. Use short sentences, avoid jargon, repeat important points such as a dip date or a disease warning, and give a contact number. WhatsApp voice notes are useful for farmers who prefer speaking to reading.

Handling difficult situations

When farmers are angry, for example about delayed support, stay calm, listen, acknowledge feelings, avoid making promises you cannot keep and explain what you will do next.

Key points

  • Communication is two-way; always seek feedback.
  • Reduce language, physical, cultural and status barriers.
  • Listen actively and use open and probing questions; avoid leading questions.
  • Prepare talks with a clear objective and a few key messages.
  • Stay calm and honest in difficult conversations.

options.text: Ask the farmer to explain the advice in their own words

quiz.question: Which is an example of an open question?

options.text: Did you dose the sheep this month?
You do clean the water troughs, don't you?
How do you feed the pigs in winter?
